docs.title: DINWEY Battery Knowledge Hub
docs.text: Official technical documentation for DINWEY truck and heavy-duty starting batteries.

docs.title: Our Mission
docs.text: This knowledge hub exists to answer one question well: how do you choose the right starting battery for a truck? We publish accurate, standards-based guidance on battery group sizes (BCI, DIN), cold cranking amps (CCA), and 12V vs 24V electrical systems — the topics commercial vehicle buyers and fleet operators ask about most.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text:
This documentation covers:

  • Selection guides — step-by-step how to choose a truck battery
  • Battery standards — BCI group sizes, DIN/EN sizes, CCA and reserve capacity
  • Electrical systems — 12V vs 24V configurations and series wiring

docs.text: Audience How they use this documentation Fleet operators Select and maintain batteries across a fleet Distributors & importers Understand specifications before placing orders OEM / private label buyers Specify the right group size and CCA for their brand Technicians Troubleshoot starting and charging issues

docs.title: 12V vs 24V Truck Electrical Systems
docs.text: TL;DR — Light trucks and pickups use 12V electrical systems; heavy trucks, semi trailers and buses use 24V systems built from two 12V batteries wired in series.

docs.title: Why Two Voltages?
docs.text:
• 12V — standard for light vehicles and light/medium trucks. Simpler, lower cost.
  • 24V — used by heavy trucks and buses because it halves the current for the same power, allowing thinner wiring and more reliable cranking of large diesel engines.

docs.title: How a 24V System Works
docs.text:
A 24V system is typically built from two 12V batteries connected in series:

Battery 1 (+) ──→ Battery 2 (−) ──→ 24V output
        (+) of battery 1 and (−) of battery 2 form the 24V terminals

In series, voltages add (12V + 12V = 24V) while the current stays the same.

Configuration Voltage Current Typical use Single 12V 12V Higher current Light trucks, pickups Two 12V in series 24V Halved current Heavy trucks, buses Two 12V in parallel 12V Doubled capacity Extended runtime

docs.title: Common Mistakes
docs.text:
• Replacing only one battery of a 24V pair — always replace both as a matched pair for balanced charging.
  • Wiring in parallel when 24V is needed — parallel doubles capacity but stays 12V.

docs.title: BCI Group Sizes Explained
docs.text: TL;DR — BCI (Battery Council International) group sizes standardize the physical footprint and terminal layout of automotive and truck batteries. For heavy-duty trucks, Group 31 is the modern standard; Group 8D and 4D are large legacy sizes.

docs.title: What Is a BCI Group Size?
docs.text: The BCI group size is a code that defines a battery's physical dimensions, terminal type and terminal orientation. It does not define the battery's electrical performance (CCA or capacity) — two Group 31 batteries can have very different CCA ratings.

docs.title: Heavy-Duty Truck Group Sizes
docs.text:
Group size Approx. dimensions (L×W×H) Typical use Notes Group 31 ~330 × 173 × 240 mm Class 7–8 trucks, off-highway Modern heavy-duty standard Group 8D ~527 × 283 × 250 mm Large trucks, generators Large, heavy legacy size Group 4D ~527 × 222 × 250 mm Large trucks, marine Large legacy size Group 65 ~306 × 192 × 192 mm Light/medium trucks Top-post automotive

Group 8D vs Group 31

Group 8D is being increasingly replaced by Group 31, which delivers comparable CCA in a smaller, lighter package. Check your battery tray before switching sizes.

docs.title: Why Group Size Matters
docs.text:
• Fit — the battery must physically fit the tray and hold-down
  • Terminals — the terminal type and position (left/right positive) must match your cables
  • Replacement — using the wrong size can damage cables or fail to secure properly

docs.title: CCA vs Group Size
docs.text: A common mistake is assuming a larger group size means more power. Group size is about dimensions; CCA is about starting power. Always verify both independently.

docs.title: Truck Battery Selection Guide
docs.text: TL;DR — Choose a truck battery in four steps: (1) confirm the group size, (2) check the cold cranking amp (CCA) requirement, (3) verify the electrical system voltage (12V or 24V), and (4) account for climate. Getting the group size and CCA wrong is the #1 cause of fleet breakdowns.

docs.title: Step 1: Confirm the Group Size
docs.text:
The group size is the physical footprint and terminal layout of the battery. It must match your vehicle's battery tray and cable reach.

Standard Common truck group sizes Market BCI Group 31, 8D, 4D North America DIN / EN H8 (L5), H9 (L6) Europe JIS Large commercial codes Japan / Asia

Always read the group size printed on your existing battery, or consult the vehicle manual.

docs.title: Step 2: Check the CCA Requirement
docs.text:
Cold cranking amps (CCA) measures a battery's ability to start an engine in cold temperatures. Diesel engines need more CCA than gasoline engines of the same size.

Truck type Typical CCA range (guidance only) Light truck / pickup 600–800 CCA Medium-duty truck 800–1000 CCA Heavy-duty / semi 850–1100+ CCA

Confirm against your manual

These are general ranges. The exact CCA requirement is printed in your vehicle manual and on the original battery label.

docs.title: Step 3: Verify the System Voltage
docs.text:
• 12V — light trucks and pickups
  • 24V — heavy trucks, semi trailers and buses (two 12V batteries in series)

Ordering the wrong voltage is a costly mistake. See the 12V vs 24V guide.

docs.title: Step 4: Account for Climate
docs.text: Colder climates require higher CCA. In extreme cold, consider AGM batteries, which perform better at low temperatures than flooded lead-acid.
